nameStory: The name 'upland cotton' comes from this plant's preference for higher, well-drained ground rather than wet lowlands where other cotton species might grow. 'Cotton' itself comes from the Arabic word 'qutun,' referring to the fluffy white fibers that burst from the seed pods like tiny clouds.
description: Upland cotton is a bushy annual plant that grows 3-6 feet tall with broad, heart-shaped leaves and showy flowers. In New England, you're most likely to encounter this as an escaped garden plant or in historical demonstration gardens, since it's not native to our region. The plant produces distinctive white, fluffy seed pods (bolls) that split open to reveal the cotton fibers we all recognize. Its yellow flowers with red centers look surprisingly similar to hibiscus blooms, which makes sense since they're in the same plant family.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The unmistakable cotton bolls - green capsules that split open to reveal fluffy white cotton fibers attached to dark seeds. The cotton feels soft and slightly oily to the touch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large, showy flowers with five cream or pale yellow petals and a deep red or maroon center. Flowers are about 2-3 inches across and have a hibiscus-like appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Broad, heart-shaped leaves with 3-5 pointed lobes, arranged alternately on the stem. Leaves feel slightly rough and fuzzy to the touch, with prominent veins.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Bushy, upright annual plant reaching 3-6 feet tall with multiple branching stems. The whole plant has a somewhat fuzzy, soft texture when you brush against it.

habitat: In New England, upland cotton is extremely rare and would only be found as an occasional garden escape or in historical/educational plantings. With only one recorded observation in our region, you might spot it near old homesteads, botanical gardens, or heritage farms where it was grown experimentally. It prefers well-drained, fertile soil and full sun.

seasonality.spring: Seeds are planted after the last frost, and young plants emerge with their distinctive lobed leaves. Early growth shows the characteristic fuzzy texture of stems and leaves.
seasonality.summer: Plants flower prolifically in mid to late summer, producing their showy yellow blooms with red centers. This is when the plant is most easily identified by its hibiscus-like flowers.
seasonality.fall: Cotton bolls mature and split open, revealing the fluffy white fibers. This is the classic 'cotton ready for harvest' stage that's most recognizable to people.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, the plant dies with the first hard frost, leaving dried brown stalks and any remaining open bolls with weathered cotton fibers.

funFact: This single species produces about 90% of all the cotton in the world - meaning that T-shirt you're wearing almost certainly came from Gossypium hirsutum, even though you're thousands of miles from the major cotton-growing regions!
confusionNotes: The flowers might be confused with hibiscus or rose of Sharon, but cotton's distinctive lobed leaves and eventual cotton bolls make identification certain. No other plant in New England produces those unmistakable fluffy white seed fibers.
contextualKnowledge: While cotton seems quintessentially Southern, it was actually grown experimentally throughout New England in colonial times before farmers realized the climate wasn't quite right for commercial production. Today's sightings are likely from heritage gardens or educational plantings rather than wild populations.
compareHints: Upland cotton is the only Gossypium species you'd encounter in New England. Within the mallow family, it's distinguished from hibiscus and rose of Sharon by its more deeply lobed leaves and, of course, its cotton-producing seed pods. Unlike its relatives that produce simple seed capsules, cotton's bolls split open to dramatically display their fluffy white fibers.
